## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
The mechanism is clear from the cross-bitwidth gradient structure.
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 has a 2-bit delta of 13.12, while the second-ranked head has delta 0.55---a $24\times$ gap ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$, $t_1/t_2{=}23.7$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's sensitivity is confined to the 2-bit operating point: its 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$.
The solver therefore has only one lever---upgrading L4H3 from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but further upgrading to 8-bit provides no additional benefit, so the budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go.
This is the ``spike'' pattern: high concentration driven by a single outlier with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.

In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth sensitivity gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern that enables meaningful budget reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

The remaining three architectures fill out the diagnostic picture.
Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$ respectively), leaving the profiler with no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.15 vs.\ $+$0.13 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit across architectures at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of top-1 to top-5 per-head 2-bit distortion (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok); $^\ddagger$standard profiling, hires pending.}
\label{tab:heterogeneity}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\
 & Ratio & Conc. & & (Uniform) & (Ours) & \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.42 & Spread \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$ & 8:1 & 0.71 & 0.90 & $+$0.20 & $+$0.20 & Spike \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.57 & 0.85 & $+$0.38 & $+$0.36 & Spike \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.24 & 0.41 & $+$0.10 & $+$0.13 & Flat \\
Gemma-2-9B$^\ddagger$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.18 & $+$0.13 & $+$0.15 & Flat \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_head_delta_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Per-head 2-bit quantization sensitivity across five architectures. Qwen2.5-7B shows high concentration in Layer-0 heads (``spread'' pattern); Yi-1.5-9B shows a single extreme outlier at Layer-4 Head-3 (``spike'' pattern); Llama-3.1-8B shows a dominant outlier at Layer-2 Head-5 (49\% of total distortion, ``spike'' pattern); Mistral-7B-v0.3 shows near-zero sensitivity across all heads; Gemma-2-9B exhibits the most uniform distribution, consistent with its low GQA ratio (2:1). Color intensity indicates PPL increase when the head is quantized to 2-bit.}
\label{fig:heatmap}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the per-head 2-bit distortion as a heatmap.
The contrast is stark: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion (dark cells) while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero; Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (34\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform---a ``spike'' that MCKP cannot exploit; Gemma-2 exhibits the most uniform heatmap across its 336 heads, consistent with its 0.23 concentration; Mistral shows similarly low distortion across all layers and heads.

\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. Mistral (0.24, $t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.18$): counterproductive.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm
from matplotlib.ticker import MaxNLocator
import numpy as np
import json
import os

plt.rcParams.update({
    'font.family': 'DejaVu Sans',
    'font.size': 11,
    'axes.titlesize': 13,
    'axes.labelsize': 12,
    'xtick.labelsize': 10,
    'ytick.labelsize': 10,
    'legend.fontsize': 10,
    'figure.dpi': 300,
    'savefig.dpi': 300,
    'savefig.bbox': 'tight',
    'savefig.pad_inches': 0.05,
    'axes.spines.top': False,
    'axes.spines.right': False,
})

OUT_DIR = '/root/ratekv/figures'

MODELS = [
    {
        'name': 'Gemma-2-9B',
        'path': '/root/ratekv/gemma2_profiling_results.json',
        'gqa': 'GQA 2:1',
        'source': 'standard',
    },
    {
        'name': 'Llama-3.1-8B',
        'path': '/root/ratekv/llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly_profiles.json',
        'gqa': 'GQA 4:1',
        'source': 'hires',
    },
    {
        'name': 'Mistral-7B-v0.3',
        'path': '/root/ratekv/mistral_ppl_profiles_hires.json',
        'gqa': 'GQA 4:1',
        'source': 'hires',
    },
    {
        'name': 'Qwen2.5-7B',
        'path': '/root/ratekv/hires_profiles.json',
        'gqa': 'GQA 7:1',
        'source': 'hires',
    },
    {
        'name': 'Yi-1.5-9B',
        'path': '/root/ratekv/yi15_hires_bf16_2bitonly_profiles.json',
        'gqa': 'GQA 8:1',
        'source': 'hires',
    },
]


def load_profiles(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        data = json.load(f)
    profiles = data.get('profiles', data)
    layer_keys = sorted([k for k in profiles if k.isdigit()], key=int)
    n_layers = len(layer_keys)
    n_heads = len(profiles[layer_keys[0]])
    delta_2bit = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads))
    for li in range(n_layers):
        for hi in range(n_heads):
            delta_2bit[li, hi] = profiles[str(li)][str(hi)]['quantization']['2']
    return delta_2bit, n_layers, n_heads


def find_top_heads(delta, n=3):
    flat = delta.flatten()
    top_idx = np.argsort(flat)[-n:][::-1]
    results = []
    for idx in top_idx:
        li, hi = divmod(idx, delta.shape[1])
        results.append((li, hi, delta[li, hi]))
    return results


def main():
    os.makedirs(OUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)

    deltas = []
    infos = []
    for m in MODELS:
        d, nl, nh = load_profiles(m['path'])
        deltas.append(d)
        infos.append((m['name'], nl, nh, m['gqa'], m['source']))

    width_ratios = [info[2] for info in infos]
    vmin, vmax = 0.005, 16

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(18, 5.8),
                              gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': width_ratios, 'wspace': 0.12})

    norm = LogNorm(vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)

    for idx, (ax, delta, (name, nl, nh, gqa, source)) in enumerate(zip(axes, deltas, infos)):
        plot_data = np.clip(delta, vmin, None)
        im = ax.imshow(plot_data, aspect='auto', origin='lower',
                       cmap='YlOrRd', norm=norm, interpolation='nearest')

        suffix = '' if source == 'hires' else '*'
        ax.set_title(f'{name}{suffix}\n({gqa}, {nl}L×{nh}H)', fontsize=10.5, pad=8)
        ax.set_xlabel('KV Head')
        if idx == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel('Layer')
        else:
            ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelleft=False)
        ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(integer=True, nbins=8))
        ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(integer=True))

        tops = find_top_heads(delta, n=1)
        li, hi, val = tops[0]
        if val > 0.5:
            ax.plot(hi, li, 'x', color='black', markersize=6, markeredgewidth=1.5)
            y_offset = -6 if li > nl * 0.3 else 6
            va = 'top' if y_offset < 0 else 'bottom'
            ax.annotate(f'L{li}H{hi}: {val:.1f}',
                        xy=(hi, li), fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold',
                        ha='center', va=va,
                        xytext=(0, y_offset), textcoords='offset points',
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.15', fc='white', ec='none', alpha=0.8))

    cbar_ax = fig.add_axes([0.92, 0.15, 0.012, 0.7])
    cbar = fig.colorbar(im, cax=cbar_ax)
    cbar.set_label('2-bit Quantization ΔPPL', fontsize=11)

    fig.text(0.01, 0.01, '* standard profiling (no hires available)', fontsize=8,
             style='italic', color='#666666')

    for fmt in ['pdf', 'png']:
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, f'fig1_head_delta_heatmap.{fmt}'),
                    bbox_inches='tight', dpi=300)
    plt.close(fig)

    print('Saved to', OUT_DIR)
    for m, d, (name, nl, nh, gqa, source) in zip(MODELS, deltas, infos):
        tops = find_top_heads(d, n=3)
        top_str = ', '.join([f'L{l}H{h}={v:.2f}' for l, h, v in tops])
        print(f'  {name} ({nl}x{nh}, {source}): {top_str}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

1	\section{Analysis}
2	\label{sec:analysis}
3	
4	\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
5	\label{sec:heterogeneity}
6	
7	The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
8	We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
9	High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.
10	
11	Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
12	The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.
13	
14	Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
The mechanism is clear from the cross-bitwidth gradient structure.
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 has a 2-bit delta of 13.12, while the second-ranked head has delta 0.55---a $24\times$ gap ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$, $t_1/t_2{=}23.7$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's sensitivity is confined to the 2-bit operating point: its 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$.
The solver therefore has only one lever---upgrading L4H3 from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but further upgrading to 8-bit provides no additional benefit, so the budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go.
This is the ``spike'' pattern: high concentration driven by a single outlier with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.

In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth sensitivity gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern that enables meaningful budget reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

The remaining three architectures fill out the diagnostic picture.
Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$ respectively), leaving the profiler with no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.15 vs.\ $+$0.13 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. When concentration falls below 0.50, the top-5\% heads contribute too little cumulative delta for the solver to construct a meaningfully non-uniform allocation; consequently the $t_1/t_5$ ratio---regardless of its value---does not alter the outcome, and concentration alone suffices to determine the category. Mistral (0.24, $t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.18$): counterproductive.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.
